questions.q: What is Pandas, and why does it matter specifically for Power BI?
options: A Python library for tabular data — Power BI can only import a Pandas DataFrame, not plain Python data of any other shape
A built-in part of Python that requires no installation
A visualization tool unrelated to data import
A replacement for Power Query that works identically
questions.explain: Pandas is the library that handles row-and-column data in Python, and it's the exact and only shape Power BI's Python integration can import — this is why Lesson 2 required installing it specifically.

questions.q: What does the line 'import pandas as pd' actually do?
options: Loads the Pandas library into the script and gives it the short, near-universal nickname pd
Installs Pandas onto the computer for the first time
Creates a new empty DataFrame automatically
Only works inside Power BI, never in a standalone Python script
questions.explain: This line loads an already-installed library (installed via pip in Lesson 2) and aliases it as pd, the near-universal convention recognized in virtually all Pandas code.

questions.q: What shape of Python data does pd.DataFrame() expect to turn into a table?
options: A dictionary where each key becomes a column and each value is a list of that column's data
A single string of comma-separated values only
A nested list with no keys at all
It can only convert data already saved as a CSV file
questions.explain: pd.DataFrame() takes a dictionary of lists (exactly the shape Lesson 5 covered) and turns each key into a column header with its list as that column's values.

questions.q: What appears down the left side of a printed DataFrame that wasn't in the original dictionary or lists?
options: The index — automatically added row numbers starting at 0
A duplicate copy of the column headers
The DataFrame's file size
A warning message about missing data
questions.explain: Pandas automatically adds a numbered index (0, 1, 2...) down the left side — something neither the dictionary nor its lists included on their own, covered in more depth in Lesson 7.

questions.q: How does this course scope 'just enough Pandas' rather than teaching the entire library?
options: It deliberately focuses on the handful of operations common in real Power BI work: reading files, cleaning, filtering, grouping, and joining
It attempts to cover every function in the Pandas library exhaustively
It only covers DataFrame creation and nothing else
It skips Pandas entirely in favor of raw Python lists
questions.explain: Pandas is large enough to be a career-length skill on its own — this course is scoped specifically to the operations that show up constantly in Power BI-adjacent work, covered across Lessons 8 through 17.
